final_answer:
>>> In a free market, the price of a good or service is determined by the interaction of supply and demand. When demand for a product increases while supply remains constant, prices tend to rise because buyers are willing to pay more to obtain the limited supply. Conversely, if supply increases while demand stays the same, prices often fall due to the greater availability of the product. The point where the supply and demand curves intersect is called the equilibrium price, which balances the quantity supplied with the quantity demanded.

>>> When a government imposes a price ceiling—setting a maximum price below the equilibrium price—it can create a shortage. Suppliers may be unwilling or unable to produce the good at the artificially low price, reducing the quantity supplied. At the same time, consumers may demand more of the product because it is cheaper, leading to a gap between the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied. This shortage can result in long lines, black markets, reduced quality of the product, or even a complete absence of the good from the market as suppliers exit the industry.
